lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: be able to describe the different structures formed by giant lattices of carbon atoms, including graphite, diamond and graphene, and discuss the applications of each

primer.text: Carbon's allotropes prove that arrangement beats ingredient: the same atoms build scratch-proof diamond, shear-easy graphite and one-atom-thin graphene. Giant covalent lattices melt ferociously high; only graphite conducts, banking one spare electron per atom; graphene inherits the sheet's talents without the stack. This note compares all three structures, bond by bond.

modules.title: One element, many personalities
sourceHeadings: Covalent bonding & giant covalent lattice structures
modules.opening: Allotropes are pure substances built from one element whose atoms connect in different arrangements - and carbon is the master of the game. Every carbon allotrope is a giant covalent lattice melting ferociously high, yet graphite shears soft while diamond scratches everything, and only graphite conducts, because only graphite leaves electrons spare.
keyPoints: Allotropes contain only one element but differ in bonding arrangement and so in physical properties.
Melting or boiling a giant covalent lattice takes very high temperatures: countless strong covalent bonds link the whole structure.
Diamond and silicon(IV) oxide are hard: breaking their 3D networks is difficult.
Graphite is soft because the forces between its carbon layers are weak.
Graphite conducts via delocalised electrons between layers; diamond's four bonded electrons leave none free.

low.restatement: Same atoms, different wiring: how the carbons connect decides whether the material melts high, scratches glass or writes on paper.
low.analogy: The same bricks build a fused dome (diamond) or stacked slabs (graphite) - construction, not ingredient, sets the behaviour.
low.examPointer: Allotrope questions are structure questions: name the bonding arrangement first, the property second.

medium.restatement: Property differences trace to connectivity and the weakest link: networks of strong covalent bonds melt high, hardness reads the 3D continuity of those bonds, and conductivity appears only where the bonding leaves electrons unassigned.
medium.analogy: One road network, three traffic rules: fully connected grids jam nothing (hard), stacked roads slide at the joins (soft), and only networks with spare lanes let current flow.
medium.examPointer: Pair every property with its structural cause - the examiner marks the cause, not the property alone.

modules.title: Graphite against diamond
modules.opening: The two heavyweight allotropes part ways at the bonding ledger. Graphite's carbons bond to three neighbours in sheets of hexagons, leaving one free electron per atom that carries current along the layers; strong in-layer bonds meet weak van der Waals forces between layers, so the sheets slide - soft, slippery, conductive. Diamond bonds every carbon to four neighbours in a tetrahedral web of identical, very strong bonds: no spare electrons, no intermolecular forces, extreme hardness.
keyPoints: Graphite bonds each carbon to three others, forming layers of hexagons with one free electron per atom.
The free electrons migrate along the layers and carry charge, so graphite conducts.
Strong covalent bonds run within the layers, but weak van der Waals forces hold layers together, letting them slide.
Diamond bonds each carbon to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement.
Diamond's bonds are all identical and very strong, with no intermolecular forces and no free electrons.

low.restatement: Graphite is three bonds plus one spare electron per atom, stacked in slick sheets; diamond is four bonds per atom, welded into one rigid web.
low.analogy: Stacks of cling film versus a welded jungle gym: the film slides and wraps, the gym neither bends nor lets anything through.
low.examPointer: Quote the bond counts - three and four - and the consequence of each in the same sentence.

medium.restatement: The allotropes diverge at the fourth electron: graphite spends three electrons on in-layer bonds and banks the fourth as a delocalised carrier between the sheets, while diamond commits all four into the tetrahedral network - conductivity, softness and hardness all follow from that single bookkeeping difference.
medium.analogy: Two pay packets: one worker keeps a third of each cheque liquid (graphite's spare electron), the other reinvests everything into a fixed structure (diamond's fourth bond).
medium.examPointer: Name the interlayer force explicitly as van der Waals' forces - 'weak forces' alone is only half the answer.

modules.title: Graphene: the single sheet
modules.opening: Graphene is graphite reduced to its minimum: one isolated layer, a continuous sheet of hexagonally bonded carbon just one atom thick. That makes it effectively a two-dimensional molecule, and its unusual behaviour - the same in-plane conduction as graphite with none of the layer weaknesses - has made it the material of choice for composite materials and electronics research.
keyPoints: Graphene is a single layer of graphite - one continuous hexagonal sheet of carbon atoms.
Its atoms are covalently bonded into one uninterrupted hexagonal layer.
Being one atom thick makes graphene essentially a 2D molecule.
Its very unusual properties suit composite materials and electronics.
It shares graphite's in-plane conduction without any stacked layers to slide.

low.restatement: Take graphite, peel off one sheet, and you have graphene: one atom-thin hexagon mesh with big electronic talents.
low.analogy: One page lifted from a ream: everything that made the ream slippery between pages is gone, leaving the page's own strengths.
low.examPointer: Anchor the definition: 'single layer of graphite' - every fuller answer hangs from that phrase.

medium.restatement: Graphene keeps graphite's per-atom ledger - three covalent bonds and one delocalised electron - but removes the interlayer van der Waals chapter entirely, so conduction and mechanical strength arrive in a strictly two-dimensional membrane.
medium.analogy: The same sheet music (bonding pattern) played by a soloist instead of a stacked choir: the harmony is identical, the physics newly pure.
medium.examPointer: Applications questions want the pair: composite materials and electronics - name both.

glossary.definition: One of the structurally different forms of the same element, such as graphite and diamond for carbon.
A structure where huge numbers of atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds throughout.
A single one-atom-thick hexagonal sheet of covalently bonded carbon atoms.
